label: O(n**2)
evidence: ReverseString recursively takes s[1..] and appends s[0] at every level -- the same shape as the 888_6 ReverseSeq trap -- so reversing a string of length L costs O(L^2), and in the worst case (one long string among the 2n inputs) this dominates the O(1)-per-character scan loops, matching the O(n**2) label under total-input-size scaling. The Python instead reverses with x[::-1], a single O(L) slice, so it is linear where the Dafny is quadratic.

label: O(n)
evidence: Each outer-loop step decreases nn by exactly power=Log2Floor(nn), and Log2Floor itself costs O(power) since its own doubling loop runs power times, so work done equals nn's decrease at every step; telescoping over the whole run gives total Dafny cost O(n) exactly. Log2Floor reimplements what Python's math.log2 does as a single O(1) library call, so Python's true cost is O(#iterations)=O(n/log n), strictly less than Dafny's O(n) -- the manual log-loop is real per-call overhead the translation introduced, though both round to the O(n) label since the vocabulary has no O(n/log n) bucket.

label: O(n**2)
evidence: ReverseSeq(doubled) recurses on s[1..] and concatenates + [s[0]] at every level, copying O(current length) per level for a total of O(n**2); the Python's D[::-1] slice reversal and the surrounding two-pointer scan are all O(n), so the label matches the Dafny only by coincidence.

label: O(n)
evidence: ReverseInts(arr) recurses via `ReverseInts(s[1..]) + [s[0]]`, the identical slice-and-concatenate-at-every-level shape flagged for ReverseSeq in 888_6, which copies O(current length) per level; since |arr| can be as large as n (a fully increasing run of a_list), this call alone is O(n**2), while the Python builds the answer with O(1) `arr.append` calls and a single O(n) `arr[::-1]` slice.
what_to_look_for: The label assumes the final reversal costs O(n) the way Python's arr[::-1] does. Open ReverseInts and confirm it is defined as `ReverseInts(s[1..]) + [s[0]]`; if the backend does not special-case that concatenation the way it does a flat loop's `s := s + [x]`, each level copies the accumulated result and the call is O(|arr|**2). Also check how large |arr| can get -- if a single test can make a_list one long increasing run, |arr| ~= n and the quadratic term dominates, so the label is too low; if |arr| is provably small for every valid input, the label could still stand.

label: O(nlogn)
evidence: firstPos := firstPos[x := i] and lastPos := lastPos[x := i] are seq updates (`s[i:=v]`) executed inside loops over |nums|=n elements; each seq update on a length-(n+1) seq copies the whole sequence, turning two O(n) loops into O(n**2), while the Python performs the equivalent first_pos[x]=i and last_pos[x]=i as O(1) in-place list assignments, keeping the Python at the labelled O(n log n) via last_pos.sort() and n bisect calls.
what_to_look_for: The label assumes firstPos/lastPos updates are O(1) as Python list assignment is. Open the two build loops and confirm the update is `firstPos := firstPos[x := i]` / `lastPos := lastPos[x := i]` on a seq<int> rather than a mutable array<int>; if it is a functional seq update, each call copies n+1 entries and the two loops are quadratic, so the Dafny (not the Python) needs the fix -- switching firstPos/lastPos to array<int> would restore O(n log n).
